passage: The playgroup room had one low shelf with a row of stuffed elephants, and four toddlers who all wanted a different one. Reena rose onto her tiptoes under the grey elephant and stretched one arm as far as it would go, grunting. Her fingers stopped a hand's width short, so she swapped arms and tried again. Beside her, Kunal jumped, tugged the shelf edge, then hauled at the rug beneath the blue elephant. When the rug slid and the elephant wobbled, he pulled the rug harder, again and again. Jyoti kept reaching for the pink elephant from exactly the same spot. A small wooden stool sat right next to her feet. Minutes passed, her face crumpled, and tears came while her arm kept stretching. Tiny Zoya tried once, then sat down with a whimper. She looked around for her mother, pointed at the yellow elephant and waited. Her mother came over and lifted it down.

qa.q: How many toddlers wanted an elephant from the shelf?
qa.a: Four toddlers each wanted a different stuffed elephant.

qa.q: How did Kunal's way of getting his elephant differ from Jyoti's?
qa.a: Kunal switched between jumping, tugging the shelf and pulling the rug, and kept using the move that made the elephant shift. Jyoti repeated one stretch from the same spot and never noticed the stool beside her.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when the tears came?
qa.a: Jyoti was frustrated and upset; her face crumpled and she cried while her arm kept stretching for the elephant.

qa.q: What small step could help Jyoti next time she cannot reach?
qa.a: A caregiver could point out the stool or invite Jyoti to try a different move, so Jyoti learns that a stuck plan can be changed. Asking for a lift, as Zoya did, is also a fine choice. 🙂

grounding: Four toddlers at one shelf show stretching, trial and error, repeating a failing move, and switching to asking for help.

passage: Lalremsiami had savings for nine months, so on a Sunday she wrote the last salary date on a calendar and counted backward. By month six, what would she need to show a funder? Every task on her list got a simple test: does it help by that date? Most did not, and she crossed them out. In Lucknow, Swati and her cofounder used a no-code tool to put together a bare invoicing screen in six weeks. They carried it to twenty Kirana shop owners before writing any backend, and took notes on which buttons confused people. Across town, Lokesh kept nudging fonts and icons in his app. Five months in, a friend asked to see it and he said, "Not yet, it isn't ready." His bank balance now covered three months, and no customer had ever touched the app. Later, Lalremsiami and her partner sat down each Friday with a sheet of spending and signups. One week the cash slipped below four months and nobody had paid, so they cancelled the paid tools, let the freelancers go, and began phoning shop owners themselves.

qa.q: How many Kirana shop owners did Swati and her cofounder show their invoicing tool to?
qa.a: They showed it to twenty Kirana shop owners in Lucknow.

qa.q: How does Lokesh's way of using his time differ from Swati's, and what did each end up with?
qa.a: Swati and her cofounder put a rough version in front of twenty users within six weeks and gained real feedback. Lokesh polished for five months with no customer, so he had no feedback and only three months of cash left.

qa.q: What might Lokesh be feeling when he tells his friend the app is not ready?
qa.a: He is probably afraid of a weak first impression and anxious about being judged, which is why he keeps delaying.

qa.q: What could Lokesh try in his last three months?
qa.a: He could show the app to a few shop owners this week, however unfinished, and hold a Friday check of spending against signups like Lalremsiami's. That would give him real feedback while cash remains. 🙂

grounding: Four founders handle a short cash runway by counting backward, shipping fast, over-polishing, and reviewing spending weekly with a cut-off point.

passage: The power went out at eight, and Harish groaned that the whole night was spoiled. The rain outside had already cancelled his picnic that afternoon, and his arms were folded. "Everything is ruined," he said. His mother put out cushions and a plate of biscuits on the living-room floor, but he stayed on the sofa, scowling at the dark window. Lavanya sat up straight in the candle light. "We can't use the tablet, but we can read by this flame, or trade tales, or sing an antakshari round," she said, counting on her fingers, and pulled her grandmother onto the cushions with her. Soon the room was full of singing. Earlier that week, the forecast had warned of a storm, so Vihaan finished his online task early and printed his notes; now he read them calmly by the candle. The day before, when rain washed out the cricket match, the neighbour's children had dragged a carrom board and a ludo set into the hall. "Different game, same fun," one of them said, striking a coin.

qa.q: What time did the power go out?
qa.a: The power went out at eight.

qa.q: How do Harish's reaction and Lavanya's reaction to the power cut differ, and what did each get out of the evening?
qa.a: Harish saw only what was lost and sat apart, so he missed the biscuits and the singing. Lavanya listed what was still possible, and she ended up singing with her grandmother.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he sat scowling at the window?
qa.a: Harish was angry and disappointed about his rained-off picnic and the dark evening, so he refused to join in.

qa.q: What could Harish's mother say or do to bring him into the evening?
qa.a: She could invite him to choose the first song or story, without pushing, so his disappointment is heard and he has a role in the fun. He might then see the evening as a different kind of day. 🙂

grounding: Children meet rain and a power cut by sulking, by listing what is still possible, by preparing early, and by switching to indoor games.

passage: Hrithik's train ticket to the new city was booked for a fortnight away, so he and his father made a list on the fridge door: admission papers, bank card, medicines, clothes, phone numbers. Each evening one more line got a tick, and the bag itself was packed the night before. Meanwhile Tejas and his parents sat with a laptop, comparing a hostel and two paying-guest rooms. He read reviews, called a senior about the walk to college, food and safety, and the family travelled there to look around before handing over any deposit. Pankaj arrived in the same city certain he would feel at home by Friday. By the third week the corridor was quiet, his phone stayed silent, and he told his mother, "I want to come back. I can't do this." Hrithik, too, ran into trouble: he skipped breakfast most mornings and read the same page three times. So he set fixed hours for meals, found a tiffin service on the next lane, and moved his study time to late evening when the hostel went quiet.

qa.q: What did Hrithik and his father put on the fridge door?
qa.a: They put up a list of things to take, including admission papers, bank card, medicines, clothes and phone numbers, and ticked one more line each evening.

qa.q: How did Tejas's preparation differ from Pankaj's expectations about the new city?
qa.a: Tejas and his parents researched, asked a senior, and visited before paying. Pankaj simply assumed he would fit in by Friday, so the lonely third week hit him hard.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he told his mother he wanted to come back?
qa.a: Pankaj felt lonely and panicked, because his expectation of quickly feeling at home had not come true.

qa.q: What could Pankaj try before deciding to leave?
qa.a: He could talk to his mother about the loneliness, then take small steps such as joining a group or greeting one neighbour each day, and give himself time to settle. If the low mood stays, he could speak to a counsellor at the college. 🤍

grounding: Students moving to a new city plan with a checklist, research housing, expect instant belonging and struggle, or adjust routines after early problems.

passage: One evening after dinner, Minakshi's family walked through their flat together, following each bedroom's route down to the stairs. Everyone practised crawling low and pressing the back of a hand against a door before opening it. Minakshi had her own way of thinking about it. "Where do we need to end up? At Mrs Rao's gate," she said. Then she went backward: out the front door, down the stairs, not the lift, and nothing carried along. In the practice run, Sumit suddenly turned around and dashed back to fetch his hamster's cage. His father caught his arm, calmly. "When the alarm rings, we leave everything, even pets, and the grown-ups do the rescuing," he said, and Sumit nodded slowly. Then Irawati noticed that the balcony door was stuck fast and a cupboard partly blocked the passage. The family dragged the cupboard aside, oiled the door, and ran the drill again and again until the whole escape took less than a minute.

qa.q: Where did Minakshi decide the family should end up?
qa.a: She decided they should end up at Mrs Rao's gate.

qa.q: How did Minakshi's planning differ from the family's walk-through, and how did the drill change the flat?
qa.a: Minakshi began at the gate and worked backward step by step, while the family walked each path from the bedrooms. The walk-through revealed the stuck balcony door and blocking cupboard, which the family then fixed.

qa.q: What was Sumit probably feeling when he ran back for the cage?
qa.a: Sumit was worried and protective about his hamster, so his urge to rescue it overrode the plan.

qa.q: What could Sumit's parents do to help him feel calmer about his hamster during a real alarm?
qa.a: They could agree beforehand that an adult will look after the hamster once everyone is out, so Sumit knows it matters and can still leave straight away. Practising that promise in the drill would help too. 🙂

grounding: A family handles home fire safety by rehearsing routes, planning backward from the meeting spot, going back for a pet in a drill, and clearing blocked exits.

passage: On the wardrobe door hung a picture chart, and every morning Tejas ticked his way down it: vest first, then shirt, then shorts, then socks and shoes. Each picture got a tick in order, and he was dressed before the milk was cool. Kishore had no chart. She said aloud, "If it is Wednesday, I wear sports shoes," and picked them up without asking anyone, because the day itself told her what to do. Mehak's morning went differently. She could only find one sock, so she climbed back into bed, pulled the blanket over her head and said, "I'm not going." Her whole morning plan seemed to have ended over one missing sock. Later that week, Kishore did up her shirt buttons one hole out and looked in the mirror. The shirt hung crooked. She frowned, undid every button and started again from the bottom one, and this time the shirt lay straight.

qa.q: What order did Tejas follow on his picture chart?
qa.a: He went in the order vest, shirt, shorts, socks, shoes.

qa.q: How did Kishore's way of knowing what to wear differ from Tejas's, and how did her buttons show another skill?
qa.a: Tejas followed a picture chart step by step, while Kishore used a rule that tied shoes to the day of the week. With the buttons she spotted a mistake, undid it and started again from the bottom.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she got back into bed?
qa.a: Mehak was frustrated and discouraged; the missing sock felt big enough to stop the whole morning, so she said she would not go.

qa.q: How could a parent help Mehak when a sock goes missing?
qa.a: A parent could stay calm and search with Mehak, or suggest another pair, so one missing item does not end the plan. Adding a step to the chart, such as checking for spares, would help next time. 🙂

grounding: Children get dressed by following a chart, by using an if-then rule, by giving up over a missing sock, and by fixing a crooked button.
